title: Quiz: Binary Arithmetic - Advanced
prompt: Test your advanced understanding of extended precision chaining, iterative multiplication logic, and flag mechanics.

questions.question: When chaining additions for extended-precision arithmetic across three 64-bit registers representing a 192-bit number, what is the correct instruction sequence for the lowest, middle, and highest bits?
options: `add`, `add`, `add`
`adds`, `adcs`, `adc`
`adc`, `adc`, `adc`
`adds`, `adds`, `adds`
questions.explanation: The lowest 64-bit addition uses `adds` so that its carry is placed in the C flag. The middle addition uses `adcs` to include that carry and set the next carry. The highest addition uses `adc` to include the final carry.
questions.hint: The first instruction needs to create the carry, the middle instruction needs to pass it along, and the last instruction only needs to consume it.

questions.question: What is the equivalent subtraction instruction sequence to `adds`, `adcs`, `adc` for extended-precision subtraction?
options: `sub`, `sbc`, `sbc`
`subs`, `sbcs`, `sbc`
`subs`, `subs`, `sub`
`sub`, `sub`, `sub`
questions.explanation: Extended-precision subtraction follows the same pattern as addition: `subs` performs the lowest-order subtraction and sets the carry/borrow information, `sbcs` includes that information in the middle subtraction, and `sbc` includes it in the final subtraction.
questions.hint: Follow the same pattern as extended-precision addition, but use the subtraction instructions.

questions.question: In the iterative multiplication algorithm for M × N, when is the multiplicand M added to the accumulator T?
options: If the highest bit of the multiplier N is 1.
If the lowest bit of the multiplier N, N[0], is 1.
On every iteration.
Only when the multiplier N is negative.
questions.explanation: At each iteration, the algorithm examines N[0], the lowest bit of the multiplier. If N[0] is 1, the multiplicand M is added to T before the arithmetic shift right.
questions.hint: The algorithm checks the rightmost bit of N on every iteration.

questions.question: What happens to the product of a binary multiplication operation in terms of register space?
options: It always overwrites the multiplicand register.
It must fit into the same number of bits as the source operands.
It may require twice as many bits as the source registers and is stored in two concatenated registers.
It automatically sets an overflow flag whenever the result exceeds 64 bits.
questions.explanation: Multiplying two N-bit values can produce a result requiring up to 2N bits. The multiplication algorithm therefore uses two concatenated registers to hold the product.
questions.hint: Think about the maximum number of bits needed when multiplying two N-bit numbers.

questions.question: Why can the signed `lt` condition not simply test whether the Negative (N) flag is 1?
options: Because N is never set by subtraction.
Because signed overflow can make the sign bit disagree with the true mathematical result, so V must also be considered.
Because the Zero flag always overrides N.
Because the Carry flag determines all signed comparisons.
questions.explanation: For signed comparisons, overflow can make the sign bit of the result misleading. The `lt` condition therefore uses `N != V` rather than testing N alone. This allows the comparison to remain correct even when signed overflow occurs.
questions.hint: The lecture defines signed `lt` as N != V. Why would checking N alone fail when overflow occurs?
